metadata.title: Finnish teachers' and students' programming motivation and their role in teaching and learning computational thinking

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICILS 2018 Finland data with a multi-stage, clustered sampling design (schools selected with PPS; students and teachers sampled within schools). To produce population-representative estimates, the authors applied sampling weights and non-response adjustments at the school level when analyzing teacher and student questionnaire responses and their associations with CT instruction emphasis and CT test scores. For variance estimation and standard errors, they used jackknife repeated replication (JRR), which is consistent with complex survey inference under ICILS design features. The manuscript does not report the exact weight variable name(s) (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly states that sampling weights and non-response adjustments were used and that jackknife repeated replication was applied.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable includes ICILS 2018 CT test scores based on five plausible values, but the manuscript does not describe how missing questionnaire or background data were handled (e.g., complete-case vs. imputation). This is a reporting gap because missingness can affect both the motivation scales and the regression samples used for CT score associations. Given the study’s reliance on weighted complex-survey estimation, the absence of a documented missing-data strategy limits reproducibility and may bias effect estimates if missingness is not ignorable.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the ICILS 2018 Finland national sample for Grade 8 students and their Grade 8 teachers. Sampling followed ICILS multi-stage design: 150 schools were randomly selected with PPS using NUTS regions; within each sampled school, 20 Grade 8 students (or all if fewer than 25) were randomly sampled; and 15 Grade 8 teachers (or all if fewer than 20) were randomly sampled. The analytic sample is the final national data in Finland (2,546 students and 1,853 teachers from 145 schools) with complex-survey weighting and jackknife repeated replication for inference.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2018 Finland Grade 8 (CT modules; plausible values) — Computational thinking (CT) test scores
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted linear regression coefficients reported: intrinsic motivation effect only for students with prior programming experience (b = 12.95, SE = 5.55, β = 0.11, p < 0.05); extrinsic motivation effect only for students without prior programming experience (b = 10.88, SE = 4.55, β = 0.08, p < 0.05). No overall model fit metrics (e.g., R²) reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Finland Grade 8 CT module data (CT test scores based on five plausible values), the study leveraged intrinsic and extrinsic programming motivation together with prior programming learning (and examined gender and home socioeconomic background as contextual factors) to predict CT test scores, finding that intrinsic motivation was positively associated with CT scores only among students with prior programming experience and extrinsic motivation was positively associated only among students without prior programming experience. This indicates that tailoring CT support to students’ prior programming exposure may improve learning outcomes, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes ICILS 2018 Finland data for Grade 8 students’ computational thinking (CT) and teachers’ CT instruction emphasis, using complex survey sampling with sampling weights and jackknife repeated replication. Students completed two of five 30-minute CIL modules and two 25-minute CT modules; CT test scores were aggregated across CT tasks and reported using five plausible values, with analyses performed separately per plausible value and then averaged. The study reports weighted descriptive statistics and linear regression associations rather than machine-learning prediction. Key results show that teachers’ intrinsic programming motivation is positively related to their CT instruction emphasis (both international CT items and programming-specific items), while extrinsic motivation shows no significant effects for experienced teachers. For students, intrinsic motivation predicts higher CT scores only among those with prior programming experience, whereas extrinsic motivation predicts higher CT scores only among those without prior experience; effect sizes are modest and the design is correlational.
